problems.title: Pair Sum in a Sorted Array

statement.description: You are given an array of integers sorted in non-decreasing order and a target. Find the two distinct indices whose values add up to the target. Return the indices in increasing order. If no pair exists, return an empty list.
statement.input_format: A sorted integer array nums and an integer target.
statement.output_format: A two-element list [left_index, right_index], or [] when no pair exists.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order

The task asks for a pair, not every pair.
When the sum is too small or too large, one endpoint can be ruled out.

brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: There are quadratically many pairs. On a large array, checking every combination repeats work that the sorted order lets us avoid.

optimal_solution.approach: Place one pointer at each end. If the sum is too small, move the left pointer right to increase it; if too large, move the right pointer left to decrease it.

problems.title: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K

statement.description: Given an integer array and an integer k, find the largest sum among all contiguous subarrays containing exactly k elements.
statement.input_format: An integer list nums and an integer k.
statement.output_format: The maximum sum of any contiguous length-k subarray.

examples.explanation: The window [5, 1, 3] has sum 9, which is the maximum.

pattern_clues: The subarray is contiguous.
Every candidate window has exactly k elements.
Adjacent windows overlap in k - 1 elements, so only one value enters and one leaves.

brute_force.approach: Compute the sum of every length-k slice independently and keep the maximum.
brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: Re-summing k elements for each starting position costs O(nk). The windows overlap heavily, so most additions are repeated.

optimal_solution.approach: Compute the first window once. For each next position, subtract the outgoing value and add the incoming value.

subgoals.title: Build the first window
subgoals.explanation: The first k values form the initial candidate.

subgoals.title: Slide one position at a time
subgoals.explanation: A shift removes exactly one value and introduces exactly one new value.

subgoals.title: Return the maximum
subgoals.explanation: Every contiguous length-k window has been visited exactly once.

optimal_solution.code:
def max_sum_subarray_k(nums, k):
    window_sum = sum(nums[i] for i in range(k))
    best = window_sum
    for right in range(k, len(nums)):
        window_sum += nums[right]
        window_sum -= nums[right - k]
        best = max(best, window_sum)
    return best

code_lines.code: window_sum = sum(nums[i] for i in range(k))
code_lines.why_this_line: Calculate the first length-k window with a generator, avoiding a temporary slice.
The first window is the best candidate until a better one is found.
Each right index is the new element entering the window.
code_lines.risk_note: Slide start index: the first k elements (0..k-1) are already summed, so sliding starts at index k.

code_lines.why_this_line: Include the incoming value.
Remove the value that has just fallen outside the window.
code_lines.risk_note: Window update: subtract the outgoing element nums[right - k] as the window advances.

code_lines.why_this_line: Compare the updated window against the best sum seen so far.
Return the maximum window sum.

Therefore each updated sum is exactly the sum of the next length-k window, and taking the maximum visits all valid windows.

statement.description: Given an n by n binary grid, find the length of the shortest clear path from the top-left to the bottom-right cell. A path may move in any of the eight directions, including diagonals, and may visit only cells containing 0. The path length is the number of visited cells, including both endpoints. Return -1 if no path exists. The grid may be modified in place to track visited cells.

constraints: Movement is allowed in all eight directions

problems.title: Open the Lock

statement.description: A lock has four wheels, each showing a digit from 0 to 9. Each move turns one wheel forward or backward by one step, with 0 and 9 wrapping around. Given a list of deadend combinations and a target, return the minimum number of moves to reach the target from "0000". A deadend state cannot be entered. Return -1 if the target cannot be reached.
statement.input_format: A list of four-character deadend strings and a four-character target string.
statement.output_format: The minimum number of wheel turns, or -1 if the target is unreachable.

examples.explanation: A shortest sequence reaches 0202 in six single-wheel turns without entering a deadend.

constraints: Each state and target has exactly four digits
The start state may itself be a deadend

pattern_clues: Each lock state is a node in an unweighted graph.
Each move changes exactly one wheel by plus or minus one with wraparound.
BFS finds the fewest moves because every move costs one.

brute_force.approach: Try every sequence of wheel turns up to increasing lengths, rejecting sequences that enter deadends.
brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: Without tracking visited states, many move sequences revisit the same combinations. The full state space contains only 10,000 states, so BFS with a visited set is efficient.
brute_force.time_complexity: Exponential in the number of moves without duplicate-state pruning

optimal_solution.approach: Run BFS from 0000. For each state, generate its eight neighbors (two turns for each of four wheels), skip deadends and visited states, and return the distance when the target is reached.
